titre: Einstein Does Not Cite Michelson-Morley in 1905
accroche: The 1887 experiment is famous. But Einstein himself said, in 1950, that he had known of it only after his 1905 paper.
contenu_vulgarise:
It is told like this: in 1887, Michelson and Morley fail to detect the Earth's motion through the ether; the result baffles physics; in 1905, Einstein answers it with relativity. It is neat. The history is less so.

## What the Experiment Measured

In Cleveland, Albert Michelson and Edward Morley mount an interferometer on a heavy stone floating on mercury: it can be rotated without a jolt, one turn in six minutes, with sixteen readings per turn. The observations are made on July 8, 9, 11, and 12, 1887, in sessions of six turns.

If the Earth were moving through a motionless ether, the fringes (the light and dark bands of the interference pattern) should have shifted by about 0.4 fringe. They read less than a twentieth of that, and probably less than a fortieth. The result is therefore not a zero, but a bound: the paper, published in the *American Journal of Science*, concludes that the relative velocity of the Earth and the ether is probably less than one sixth of the Earth's orbital velocity.

## What Einstein Says About It

The 1905 paper, “On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies,” names neither Michelson nor Morley. It speaks of unsuccessful attempts to detect a motion of the Earth relative to the “light medium,” without saying which.

The physicist Robert Shankland, of the Case Institute in Cleveland, visits Einstein at Princeton five times between 1950 and 1954 and notes his remarks immediately afterward. On February 4, 1950, Einstein tells him he knew of the experiment through Lorentz's writings, but only after 1905: otherwise, he would have cited it in his paper. The results that had influenced him most, he adds, were stellar aberration and Fizeau's measurement of the speed of light in moving water. That was enough for him, he says.

On October 24, 1952, the tone changes. Einstein no longer knows when he heard of it and did not feel directly influenced by it during the seven years that relativity occupied him: he took the result to be true. Afterward, he thought about it a great deal between 1905 and 1909, and concludes that he had already been aware of it before 1905, partly through Lorentz's papers, and even more because he had simply taken the result to be true. Shankland points out that these remarks come from memory, about facts half a century old.

## An Important Experiment, Not a Starting Point

This does not make the experiment a detail. When Shankland tells him that it was once judged a failure, Einstein protests: no one should have said that; many negative results are not very important, but Michelson's is a very great result, one that everyone should understand. But the textbook story puts in order a sequence that Shankland's reported remarks do not describe: in them, Einstein does not present the experiment as the starting point of his theory.

When a physicist takes a result for granted without thinking about it, since when has he known it?

repere.texte: On February 4, 1950, Einstein tells Robert Shankland that he knew of the Michelson-Morley experiment only after 1905: “Otherwise, I would have mentioned it in my paper.”
repere.source: R. S. Shankland, “Conversations with Albert Einstein,” American Journal of Physics 31, 47-57 (1963), notes taken after each visit

carte.punch: In 1950, Einstein says he did not know of Michelson-Morley before 1905.
carte.idee: The 1887 experiment measured a shift of less than a twentieth of the one expected. Einstein said he learned of it after his 1905 paper, then, in 1952, that he had always taken the result to be true. The textbook story is neater than the history.

quiz.question: What does Einstein tell Shankland, in 1950, about the Michelson-Morley experiment and his 1905 paper?
choix: That he knew of it only after 1905; otherwise, he would have cited it in his paper
That it pushed him to write the paper, as the textbooks teach
That he had redone it himself to check the result before writing
That he judged it a failure, with no consequence for physics
quiz.explication: In 1950, Einstein says he would have mentioned it had he known of it; in 1952, he qualifies this, without saying it had pushed him to write. Nor did he judge the experiment unimportant: according to Shankland, he felt that no one should have called it a failure, that it was a very great result.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What result do Michelson and Morley obtain in 1887?
choix: A shift of 0.4 fringe, as the ether predicts
An exactly zero shift, without the slightest uncertainty
A shift of less than a twentieth of the one expected, probably a fortieth
A shift too irregular to be interpreted
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The result is an upper bound, not an exact zero: less than a twentieth of what the ether predicted, probably less than a fortieth. A shift of 0.4 fringe is what was expected, not what was read.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which observations does Einstein cite in 1950 as the most influential on him?
choix: Rømer's measurements of the speed of light
Maxwell's work on the magnetism of the planets
Stellar aberration and Fizeau's measurement in moving water
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to Shankland's notes, Einstein names stellar aberration and Fizeau's measurements of light in moving water: that was enough for him. Michelson-Morley is not on his 1950 list.
